Regular investing: average quoted price is different from your cost per unit

Track six equal cash purchases through fractional units, arithmetic and harmonic averages, fixed transaction fees and a separate market valuation in four interactive charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reconcile six equal cash purchases with fractional units and one fee per order

Interactive planning lab

Arithmetic average of the six execution prices$18.33
Purchase-price amount divided by total units$17.49
All household cash spent divided by total units$17.67

Six original hypothetical monthly executions buy the same fictional asset with equal household cash each time. A fixed fee is paid from that cash before buying fractional units at the stated price. At 100% variation, prices are the selected base multiplied by 1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2 and 1; zero variation makes all six prices identical. Other variation settings scale only those authored deviations from the base. A separate valuation price is applied after purchase six. All three headline metrics are CAD per unit, not dollar balances or percentage returns. Fractional units are unrestricted and calculations retain precision. No dividends, splits, cash interest, spreads, price impact, currency changes, sale fees, tax, account limits or market forecasts are included. All-in cash per unit is an accounting comparison, not a determination of tax ACB. No lump-sum strategy, equal-unit strategy, annualized return or historical performance is calculated.

The central idea

Divide the relevant cash amount by the units actually acquired. A lower purchase-price average than the arithmetic average does not establish a profit or a superior investing schedule.

01

Give the cash and the units their own records

Suppose you invest the same cash amount every month while the unit price changes. Averaging the quoted prices gives each month equal weight. Dividing your purchase spending by your acquired units gives a different average because a lower price allows the same cash to buy more units.

The distinction is arithmetic, not evidence that a particular schedule is profitable. A useful record identifies execution prices, cash available, charges, units bought and the price later used to value those units.

Investor.gov’s dollar-cost-averaging explanation describes equal purchases at regular intervals and the resulting change in units when prices move. This article uses that mechanism in six original monthly transactions. It does not compare investing an existing lump sum with investing future earnings.

The default assigns CAD 200 to each purchase, including a CAD 2 transaction fee. Net security-purchase cash is therefore CAD 198 per order. The six execution prices are CAD 20, 16, 12, 18, 24 and 20 per unit. These are authored numbers, not observations from a fund.

02

Follow each execution before calculating an average

At CAD 20, net cash of CAD 198 buys 9.9 units. At CAD 16 it buys 12.375 units; at CAD 12, 16.5 units. The fourth, fifth and sixth purchases add 11, 8.25 and 9.9 units respectively.

Total units are 67.925. Security-purchase spending is six times CAD 198, or CAD 1,188. Fees total CAD 12, bringing total household cash spent to CAD 1,200.

The unit bars make the changing quantities visible. They should not be interpreted as changes in the amount the household saved: each monthly cash assignment is still CAD 200. The fee is paid from that assignment before the units are acquired.

The example allows any fractional unit amount and retains calculation precision. Actual brokers, plans or securities may impose whole-unit orders, rounding rules or minimums. Those restrictions would require a separate cash-residue ledger and could change the units obtained.

03

Identify the numerator before reporting a unit cost

The simple arithmetic average of the six execution prices is their sum divided by six: CAD 110 ÷ 6, or approximately CAD 18.33 per unit. It describes this list of prices, with equal weight assigned to every purchase date.

The actual purchase-price amount per acquired unit is CAD 1,188 ÷ 67.925, or approximately CAD 17.49. This is a unit-weighted average: multiplying each execution price by its purchased units reconstructs the CAD 1,188 security spending.

Total household cash per unit includes the fees. CAD 1,200 ÷ 67.925 is approximately CAD 17.67. It exceeds the purchase-price average because the same acquired units must account for an additional CAD 12 of cash spent.

The three headline figures are all CAD per unit. None is an account balance or a percentage investment return. The line chart traces their cumulative versions after each purchase so a reader can see how the records develop, rather than replacing the underlying transactions with one unexplained average.

04

Use the harmonic mean only when its equal-cash condition holds

Write the six positive prices as P₁ through P₆ and equal net purchase cash as C. Total units are C ÷ P₁ + C ÷ P₂ + … + C ÷ P₆. Total security spending is 6C.

Dividing spending by units cancels C and gives 6 ÷ (1/P₁ + 1/P₂ + … + 1/P₆). This is the harmonic mean of the six positive prices, matching the definition in NIST’s harmonic-mean reference.

The identity applies here because equal household cash and an identical fixed fee leave equal net cash at every execution. If the amounts or fees vary between purchases, calculate total actual spending divided by total actual units directly. An unweighted harmonic mean would then generally answer a different question.

For positive prices, the harmonic mean is no greater than the arithmetic mean, with equality when all the prices are identical. That mathematical comparison is between two averages of the same price list. It does not compare this schedule’s realized return with another strategy, and it does not remove the effect of charges.

05

Reconcile the separate valuation without treating costs as profit

The valuation input is independent of the six execution prices. At the default CAD 20 per unit, the 67.925 units have market value of CAD 1,358.50. Compared with CAD 1,200 of household cash spent, the unrealized cash gain is CAD 158.50.

The waterfall starts with that CAD 1,200, subtracts the CAD 12 paid in fees and adds CAD 170.50 of price change across the purchased units. The resulting CAD 1,358.50 is the market value, with the fee deducted once.

Change only the valuation price to CAD 15. Market value becomes CAD 1,018.875 before display rounding, and the unrealized cash result becomes a loss of CAD 181.125. The six-price arithmetic average and purchase-price harmonic mean have not changed. A purchase average below an arithmetic average can therefore coexist with an investment loss.

The separate valuation is not an executed sale. Selling costs, tax and access to cash remain outside the illustration. The all-in cash figure is not a determination of the asset’s tax adjusted cost base.

06

Test identical prices and fee drag before drawing a conclusion

The variation control scales the authored deviations from the first-price base. At 100%, the default six-price shape is 1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2 and 1 times the base. Zero variation makes all execution prices equal. Changing it does not select a historical market episode or assign probabilities to a decline.

With zero variation, a CAD 20 price and the unchanged CAD 2 fee, every purchase buys 9.9 units. Both the arithmetic price and the purchase-price average are CAD 20, while household cash per unit is approximately CAD 20.20. Valuing the units at CAD 20 leaves a CAD 12 loss, exactly equal to the six fees.

The signed matrix changes the valuation price and fee while preserving the selected execution prices and monthly cash. Its rows are explicit comparison prices, not confidence bounds. A larger fee reduces the units bought from the fixed budget; a higher valuation price raises their market value.

FINRA’s discussion of regular investing identifies transaction costs and the distinction between existing cash and money invested as it is earned. Those practical considerations require their own records. This calculation supplies neither a guarantee of profit nor an allocation or timing recommendation.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical charts use six authored execution prices, equal monthly cash, unrestricted fractional units and a fixed fee paid from each purchase budget. They are neither a backtest nor a comparison of available investment products. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
